big_ideas.title: IT creates value only through the business
big_ideas.text: Technology pays off when it changes a process, decision or product; an investment is judged by the business outcome it enables, in money and risk.

big_ideas.title: Strategy, architecture and governance must line up
big_ideas.text: Decision rights, the enterprise architecture and the portfolio translate business strategy into systems; misalignment shows up as duplicate systems, shadow IT and stranded spend.

big_ideas.title: Risk is managed, never eliminated
big_ideas.text: Security, continuity and compliance are trade-offs priced against impact and likelihood, with controls chosen to bring residual risk inside appetite.

big_ideas.title: Data is an organisational asset
big_ideas.text: Data has owners, quality, lineage and a lifecycle; its value depends on governance and integration as much as on storage technology.

big_ideas.title: Information systems are sociotechnical
big_ideas.text: People, process and technology change together; adoption, incentives and ethics decide whether a technically sound system succeeds.

practices.title: Frame the business problem
practices.text: State the goal, stakeholders, constraints and what decision the analysis supports.

practices.title: Quantify
practices.text: Put numbers on value, cost, risk, schedule and service levels — NPV, TCO, ALE, EVM, availability.

practices.title: Model
practices.text: Represent processes, data, architecture and requirements in a standard notation (BPMN, ER, capability map, use case).

practices.title: Choose and justify
practices.text: Compare options against explicit criteria and recommend one, naming the trade-off accepted.

practices.title: Govern and control
practices.text: Assign decision rights, controls, metrics and review cycles so the choice stays on track.

practices.title: Weigh people and ethics
practices.text: Account for adoption, change, privacy, fairness, law and sustainability.

los.do: Classify a described system by its strategic role (cost leadership, differentiation, focus) and the Porter value-chain activity it changes.
ek: IT advantage lasts only if hard to copy — complementary processes and data, not the technology itself.

los.do: Place each application of a portfolio in the McFarlan grid (support, factory, turnaround, strategic) from its current and future impact.
ek: Strategic = high current and future impact; factory = high current, low future; the quadrant sets how it should be governed and funded.

los.do: Compute NPV, ROI and payback period of an IT project from its cash flows and discount rate, and accept or reject it.
ek: NPV = Σ CF_t/(1 + r)^t − I₀; accept if NPV > 0; payback ignores the time value of money and later flows.

los.do: Compute total cost of ownership over a horizon for build, buy (licence) and SaaS options, including hidden costs.
ek: TCO = acquisition + implementation + operation + support + exit; licences are often < 30% of TCO.

los.do: Rank a set of proposed projects by a weighted scoring model under a budget constraint.
ek: Score = Σ weight × rating; pick in score-per-cost order until the budget binds, checking dependencies.

los.do: Assign decision rights for an IT decision domain (principles, architecture, infrastructure, applications, investment) to a governance archetype for a scenario.
ek: Weill & Ross archetypes: business monarchy, IT monarchy, federal, duopoly, feudal, anarchy; investment is usually business-led.

los.do: Match a governance need to the framework that addresses it — COBIT, ITIL, ISO/IEC 27001, NIST CSF, TOGAF.
ek: COBIT governs and audits IT overall; ITIL runs services; 27001 certifies an ISMS; NIST CSF organises cyber risk; TOGAF develops architecture.

los.do: Build a RACI matrix for a described process and find its defects (no A, several A's, no R).
ek: Exactly one Accountable per activity; at least one Responsible; Consulted is two-way, Informed one-way.

los.do: Assign an artefact or decision to its architecture domain (business, data, application, technology) and to the TOGAF ADM phase that produces it.
ek: ADM: Preliminary, A Vision, B Business, C Information Systems (data + application), D Technology, E Opportunities, F Migration, G Governance, H Change.

los.do: Build a capability map for a described organisation and mark the capabilities where heat-mapped investment should go.
ek: Capabilities say what the business does, independent of org chart and systems; they are stable while processes change.

los.do: Classify applications as Tolerate, Invest, Migrate or Eliminate from their business value and technical fit.
ek: Gartner TIME: high value + good fit ⇒ invest; high value + poor fit ⇒ migrate; low + good ⇒ tolerate; low + poor ⇒ eliminate.

los.do: Choose an integration style (file transfer, shared database, API/RPC, messaging, event streaming) for a described pair of systems and count point-to-point links avoided by a hub.
ek: n systems point-to-point need n(n − 1)/2 links; a bus or hub needs n; asynchronous messaging decouples availability.

los.do: Identify which migration strategy a cloud move uses (rehost, replatform, refactor, repurchase, retire, retain) from its description.
ek: Rehost = lift-and-shift; refactor rewrites for cloud-native; repurchase moves to SaaS.

los.do: Model a described business process in BPMN with pools, lanes, gateways and events, and spot the hand-off that causes delay.
ek: Exclusive gateway = one path; parallel = all paths; message flows cross pools, sequence flows stay inside one.

los.do: Write a use case (actor, preconditions, main flow, extensions) or user stories with acceptance criteria from an interview transcript.
ek: Story = as a <role> I want <goal> so that <benefit>; INVEST: independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable.

los.do: Prioritise a requirement list with MoSCoW or Kano and justify which items fall out of a release.
ek: Must / Should / Could / Won't (this time); Kano: basic, performance and delighter features age into basics.

los.do: Find the critical path, project duration and each activity's slack from an activity-on-node network — auto-checked.
ek: Forward pass gives earliest start/finish, backward pass latest; slack = LS − ES; zero-slack activities form the critical path.

los.do: Compute earned-value metrics (PV, EV, AC, CV, SV, CPI, SPI, EAC) from a status report and say whether the project is over budget or late.
ek: CPI = EV/AC, SPI = EV/PV; < 1 means over cost or behind; EAC = BAC/CPI if the trend continues.

los.do: Choose a delivery approach (predictive, agile, hybrid) and a deployment strategy (big bang, phased, parallel, pilot, blue-green, canary) for a described rollout.
ek: Parallel running costs most and risks least; canary exposes a small share of users first; regulated or fixed-scope work leans predictive.

los.do: Capture a scenario's data requirements as a conceptual model and choose the data-management technology the domain needs.
ek: Conceptual (entities, relationships) → logical (tables, keys) → physical; the access pattern and consistency need pick the store.

los.do: Compute data-quality scores (completeness, validity, uniqueness, timeliness) for a sample table and name the root cause of the worst one.
ek: Completeness = non-null / total; uniqueness = distinct keys / rows; quality problems are fixed at the source process, not downstream.

los.do: Assign data owner, steward and custodian roles for a data domain and write the policy decision each makes.
ek: Owner is accountable (business); steward defines meaning and quality rules; custodian (IT) operates storage and access.

los.do: Design a star schema for a described analytic question: declare the grain, the fact table measures and the dimensions.
ek: State the grain first; facts are additive numeric measures at that grain; dimensions carry descriptive attributes, denormalised.

los.do: Choose the slowly-changing-dimension type (1, 2, 3) for an attribute whose history does or doesn't matter, and show the resulting rows.
ek: Type 1 overwrites; type 2 adds a new row with effective dates and a surrogate key; type 3 keeps a previous-value column.

los.do: Choose between ETL into a warehouse, ELT into a lakehouse and streaming ingestion for a described data volume, variety and latency need.
ek: ELT pushes transformation to scalable storage; streaming fits seconds-level latency; schema-on-read trades governance for flexibility.

los.do: Write the SQL aggregation that answers a business question over a star schema — auto-checked by result set.
ek: Join the fact to the needed dimensions, filter on dimension attributes, GROUP BY the reporting level.

los.do: Match a business question to descriptive, diagnostic, predictive or prescriptive analytics and to a method (dashboard, cohort, regression, classification, optimisation).
ek: Descriptive = what happened; diagnostic = why; predictive = what will; prescriptive = what to do.

los.do: Compute the expected profit of acting on a classifier's predictions from its confusion matrix and the cost of each error.
ek: Expected value = Σ count × payoff per cell; the best threshold depends on error costs, not accuracy.

los.do: Define a KPI for a described objective with formula, target, owner and data source, and flag a vanity metric.
ek: A KPI ties to a decision and has a target; vanity metrics (raw sign-ups, page views) move without changing outcomes.

los.do: Size the servers or cloud instances a described workload needs at peak with headroom, and the cost of each option.
ek: Capacity = peak demand / (per-unit capacity × target utilisation); size for peak, not average.

los.do: Choose IaaS, PaaS, SaaS or on-premises for a described system and state who manages each layer under the shared-responsibility model.
ek: The provider takes more layers as you move IaaS → PaaS → SaaS; data and identity stay the customer's responsibility in every model.

los.do: Recommend in-house, outsourced, offshored or cloud sourcing for a function using transaction-cost reasoning.
ek: Outsource commodity, well-specified work; keep asset-specific, strategic, hard-to-monitor work inside.

los.do: Classify a described event as an incident, problem, service request or change, and the change as standard, normal or emergency.
ek: Incident = restore service fast; problem = find the root cause; standard changes are pre-approved and low-risk.

los.do: Compute SLA attainment, MTTR and allowed downtime from an incident log and decide whether a credit is owed.
ek: Availability = (agreed time − downtime) / agreed time; MTTR = total repair time / incidents.

los.do: Prioritise an incident from its impact and urgency using a priority matrix.
ek: Priority = f(impact, urgency): high/high = P1; priority sets the response and resolution targets.

los.do: Choose a vendor by a weighted evaluation of a set of RFP responses and name the contract terms that protect exit.
ek: Weight criteria before scoring; protect exit with data-portability, termination-assistance and escrow clauses.

los.do: Score risks on a likelihood × impact matrix and choose a treatment (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) for each.
ek: Inherent risk before controls, residual after; accept only within the stated risk appetite.

los.do: Compute ALE before and after a proposed control and its return on security investment.
ek: ROSI = (ALE_before − ALE_after − control cost) / control cost.

los.do: Classify a control as preventive, detective or corrective and administrative, technical or physical.
ek: Defense in depth layers control types so one failure is caught by another.

los.do: Derive RTO and RPO for a business process from a business-impact analysis, and pick the recovery site and backup frequency that meet them.
ek: RPO = tolerable data loss ⇒ backup or replication interval; RTO = tolerable downtime ⇒ hot, warm or cold site.

los.do: Compute what a full, incremental or differential backup schedule must restore after a failure on a given day, and the worst-case data loss.
ek: Incremental restore = last full + every incremental since; differential = last full + latest differential; loss = time since last backup.

los.do: Map a described control to its NIST CSF 2.0 function (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover).
ek: Govern was added in 2.0 for strategy and supply-chain risk; the functions run concurrently, not as a sequence.

los.do: Identify the segregation-of-duties conflict in a described set of user roles and propose the compensating control.
ek: No one person should both initiate and approve, or both hold assets and record them; where SoD can't be split, add review.

los.do: Predict adoption of a described system from TAM/UTAUT factors and name the intervention that raises it.
ek: Perceived usefulness and ease of use drive intention; UTAUT adds social influence and facilitating conditions.

los.do: Place a described organisation's change effort in a change model (Lewin, Kotter, ADKAR) and name the step it skipped.
ek: Kotter: urgency, coalition, vision, communicate, empower, short-term wins, consolidate, anchor; skipping urgency stalls most efforts.

los.do: Locate a technology's adopters on the diffusion curve and decide how to cross the chasm to the early majority.
ek: Innovators 2.5%, early adopters 13.5%, early majority 34%; the early majority buys whole-product solutions and references.

los.do: Fill a business model canvas for a described digital venture and identify its riskiest assumption.
ek: Nine blocks: segments, value proposition, channels, relationships, revenue, resources, activities, partners, costs; test the riskiest first.

los.do: Compute customer lifetime value and CAC payback for a subscription product and decide whether growth is profitable.
ek: LTV ≈ ARPU × gross margin / churn; healthy SaaS often wants LTV/CAC ≥ 3 and payback < 12 months.

los.do: Identify the network effects (direct, indirect/two-sided) in a platform and the side to subsidise.
ek: Subsidise the side whose participation most attracts the other and that is more price-sensitive.

los.do: Determine whether GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, HIPAA or FERPA applies to a described data flow and the lawful basis or consent it needs.
ek: GDPR follows EU data subjects; CCPA/CPRA covers qualifying businesses handling California residents' data; HIPAA covers health data of covered entities; FERPA covers education records.

los.do: Decide when a data-protection impact assessment is required and list the privacy-by-design measures for a described system.
ek: High-risk processing (large-scale sensitive data, profiling, monitoring) needs a DPIA; minimise, pseudonymise, limit retention, default to private.

los.do: Analyse a described IS decision with stakeholder, utilitarian and rights-based reasoning and recommend an action.
ek: Identify every affected stakeholder; consequences and duties can disagree — state which one governs and why.

los.do: Compare the lifetime carbon and cost of keeping versus refreshing a hardware fleet, including embodied emissions.
ek: Embodied carbon of manufacture often exceeds years of use-phase emissions for end-user devices; extending life is usually greener.
